facts.fact_text: On 5 December 2011 the applicants took part in a public demonstration (a meeting) at Chistyye Prudy, Moscow.
The public demonstration on 5 December 2011 was held to protest against the allegedly rigged State Duma elections.
The demonstration on 5 December 2011 had been duly authorised by the mayor of Moscow.
The number of participants at the meeting on 5 December 2011 was estimated between 5,000 and 10,000.
The meeting on 5 December 2011 was conducted by the second applicant.
During the meeting on 5 December 2011, the first applicant addressed the participants with a speech calling for fresh, fair elections.
During the meeting on 5 December 2011, the first applicant described United Russia, the election frontrunner, as "a party of crooks and thieves".
According to the applicants, no one in the surrounded group put up any resistance.
The applicants claimed that the surrounded group chanted "One for all, and all for one!".
After the demonstration on 5 December 2011, the applicants were arrested.
The applicants claimed that their way was suddenly blocked by the riot police (сотрудники внутренних войск и ОМОН).
The applicants claimed that without any introduction or demand, the police surrounded a group of about one hundred protesters, including the applicants, pressing them against a building.
The applicants claimed that the surrounded group chanted "One for all, and all for one!".
The applicants claimed that the riot police then began to arrest the protesters.
The applicants claimed that they obeyed the police and followed them to the police bus.

According to the Government, at the end of the meeting the second applicant called on the participants to march down Myasnitskaya Street onto Lubyanskaya Square and then to the office of the Central Electoral Commission.
According to the Government, at 8.30 p.m. about sixty people, including the applicants, began walking down Chistoprudnyy Boulevard, Bolshaya Lubyanka Street and Rozhdestvenka Street.
According to the Government, the group of about sixty people walked along the road, obstructing the traffic and chanting slogans such as "This is our city!" and "Down with the police state!".
According to the Government, at the crossroads of Pushechnaya and Rozhdestvenka Streets the police blocked the march and ordered the marchers to stop.
According to the Government, the marchers pushed through the police cordon at the crossroads of Pushechnaya and Rozhdestvenka Streets and went on.
According to the Government, the marchers were stopped by the police again at 2 Teatralnyy Proyezd.
According to the Government, the marchers ignored the repeated demands of the police to stop and thereby prevented the police from carrying out their mission of securing public order.
According to the Government, confronted with the marchers' persistent behaviour, the police arrested the applicants.
Both applicants were arrested at about 8.45 p.m. on 5 December 2011.
Both applicants were taken to a police bus after their arrest.
At about 9.40 p.m. on 5 December 2011 the applicants were taken to the Severnoye Izmaylovo District police station, Moscow.
At 11.40 p.m. on 5 December 2011 the first applicant was subjected to a body search at the Severnoye Izmaylovo District police station, which lasted until 12.15 a.m.
The first applicant's personal affairs, including his mobile phone, barrister licence, watch, money, credit cards, driving licence and some items of clothing, were seized during the body search.

The second applicant was searched at the Severnoye Izmaylovo District police station, and his mobile phone, belt, watch, whistle and a badge reading "Against the Party of Crooks and Thieves" were seized.
The list of the seized objects from both applicants was recorded in the search report.
The applicants were unable to retrieve the seized objects, although those objects were not attached to the case file.
The demonstration on 5 December 2011 had been duly authorised by the mayor of Moscow.

The Federal Law on Assemblies, Meetings, Demonstrations, Marches and Picketing (no. 54-FZ of 18 August 2004) provided, at the material time, that a public event could be stopped if there was a real threat to life or the physical integrity of persons or property.

The Federal Law on Assemblies, Meetings, Demonstrations, Marches and Picketing (no. 54-FZ of 18 August 2004) provided, at the material time, that a public event could be stopped if the participants had acted unlawfully or the event organiser had knowingly breached the requirements of the Act as regards the conduct of the event (section 16).

Under the Federal Law on Assemblies, Meetings, Demonstrations, Marches and Picketing (no. 54-FZ of 18 August 2004), a representative of the public authority, who had to be present at the event, could order the event organiser to put an end to the event in circumstances justifying stopping the event.

Under the Federal Law on Assemblies, Meetings, Demonstrations, Marches and Picketing (no. 54-FZ of 18 August 2004), the representative of the public authority had to explain the reasons for the order to end the event and provide time for compliance with it.

Under the Federal Law on Assemblies, Meetings, Demonstrations, Marches and Picketing (no. 54-FZ of 18 August 2004), if the organiser did not comply with the order to end the event, the public official could issue the same order to the participants.

Under the Federal Law on Assemblies, Meetings, Demonstrations, Marches and Picketing (no. 54-FZ of 18 August 2004), if both the organiser and participants failed to comply with the order to end the event, the police were to take appropriate measures to stop the event (section 17).

Article 19.3 of the Code of Administrative Offences of 30 December 2001, at the material time, provided that failure to obey a lawful order or demand of a police officer in connection with the performance of their official duties related to maintaining public order and security, or impeding the performance by them of their official duties, shall be punishable by a fine of between 500 and 1,000 Russian roubles or by administrative detention of up to fifteen days.

Article 20.2(1) of the Code of Administrative Offences of 30 December 2001, at the material time, provided that breaches of the established procedure for the organisation of public gatherings, meetings, demonstrations, marches or pickets shall be punishable by an administrative fine of between ten and twenty times the minimum wage, payable by the organisers.

Article 20.2(2) of the Code of Administrative Offences of 30 December 2001, at the material time, provided that breaches of the established procedure for the conduct of public gatherings, meetings, demonstrations, marches or pickets shall be punishable by an administrative fine of between 1,000 and 2,000 Russian roubles for the organisers, and between 500 and 1,000 Russian roubles for the participants.

Article 27.2(1) of the Code of Administrative Offences of 30 December 2001 provided that the escorting or the transfer by force of an individual for the purpose of drawing up an administrative offence report, if this cannot be done at the place where the offence was discovered and if the drawing up of a report is mandatory, shall be carried out by the police.
Article 27.2(2) of the Code of Administrative Offences of 30 December 2001 provided that the escort operation shall be carried out as quickly as possible.

Article 27.2(3) of the Code of Administrative Offences of 30 December 2001 provided that the escort operation shall be recorded in an escort operation report, an administrative offence report or an administrative detention report, and that the escorted person shall be given a copy of the escort operation report if he or she so requests.

Article 27.3(1) of the Code of Administrative Offences of 30 December 2001 provided that administrative detention or short-term restriction of an individual's liberty may be applied in exceptional cases if this is necessary for the prompt and proper examination of the alleged administrative offence or to secure the enforcement of any penalty imposed by a judgment concerning an administrative offence.

Article 27.3(3) of the Code of Administrative Offences of 30 December 2001 provided that where the detained person so requests, his family, the administrative department at his place of work or study and his defence counsel shall be informed of his whereabouts.

Article 27.3(5) of the Code of Administrative Offences of 30 December 2001 provided that the detained person shall have his rights and obligations under the Code explained to him, and the corresponding entry shall be made in the administrative arrest report.
Article 27.4(1) of the Code of Administrative Offences of 30 December 2001 provided that administrative detention shall be recorded in a report.
Article 27.4(2) of the Code of Administrative Offences of 30 December 2001 provided that if he or she so requests, the detained person shall be given a copy of the administrative detention report.

Article 27.5(1) of the Code of Administrative Offences of 30 December 2001 provided that the duration of administrative detention shall not exceed three hours, except in the cases set out in paragraphs 2 and 3 of that Article.

Article 27.5(2) of the Code of Administrative Offences of 30 December 2001 provided that persons subject to administrative proceedings concerning offences involving unlawful crossing of the Russian border may be subject to administrative detention for up to 48 hours.

Article 27.5(3) of the Code of Administrative Offences of 30 December 2001 provided that persons subject to administrative proceedings concerning offences punishable, among other administrative sanctions, by administrative detention may be subject to administrative detention for up to 48 hours.

Article 27.5(4) of the Code of Administrative Offences of 30 December 2001 provided that the term of the administrative detention is calculated from the time when a person escorted in accordance with Article 27.2 is taken to the police station, and in respect of a person in a state of alcoholic intoxication, from the time of his sobering up.

The applicants claimed that the conditions of detention during their transfer between the police stations were inhuman and degrading.
The applicants claimed that the conditions of detention in the cell at the Kitay-Gorod District police station were inhuman and degrading.
The applicants claimed that they had spent six hours being driven to different police stations without being given any food or drinking water.

The applicants claimed that at the Kitay-Gorod District police station they were placed together in a cell measuring about 6 sq. m with concrete walls, a metal grill, a concrete floor, no windows and no furniture except for two narrow wooden benches.
The applicants claimed that the cell at the Kitay-Gorod District police station was poorly lit and had no ventilation.
The applicants claimed that there was no sanitary equipment, beds or bedding in the cell at the Kitay-Gorod District police station.

The applicants claimed that they did not receive any food or water until later on 6 December 2011 when they were allowed to receive a parcel from their families containing drinking water and crackers.
The applicants claimed that no food other than drinking water and crackers was allowed in the parcels from their families.
The Government submitted that the applicants had spent about one hour in transit to the Vostochnyy District police station.
The Government submitted that the applicants had spent about forty-five minutes in transit to the Kitay-Gorod District police station.
The Government submitted that the transit times were not long enough to require the provision of meals.

According to the Government, the applicants were detained at the Kitay-Gorod District police station in an administrative-detention cell measuring 12.3 sq. m equipped with artificial lighting and mandatory ventilation.
The Government claimed that the applicants had been provided with a sleeping place — a wooden bench — and bedding, which they had refused.

The Government provided a photograph of the cell at the Kitay-Gorod District police station with a metal grill, a close-up photograph of the bench showing its width of 47 cm, and another photograph showing the same bench covered with a blanket and with a pillow placed on it.

The Government contended that the cells at the Kitay-Gorod District police station had to be cleaned and disinfected twice a day and that pest control had to be carried out once every three months, in accordance with the cleaning service agreement between the Ministry of the Interior and a private company.
The Government provided a copy of the cleaning service agreement between the Ministry of the Interior and a private company in support of their statement about cell cleaning and disinfection.
The Government alleged that the applicants had not complained about the conditions of their detention at the Kitay-Gorod District police station.
According to the Government, the applicants had been offered food at the Kitay-Gorod District police station but had refused to take it.

The Tverskoy District Court of Moscow dismissed the defence arguments concerning the unlawful deprivation of liberty during six hours as unsubstantiated, noting that after his arrest at Teatralnyy Proyezd, at 2.30 a.m. on 6 December 2011 the first applicant was taken to the Kitay-Gorod District police station where the administrative material against him was issued.
The Tverskoy District Court of Moscow held that the police officers had complied with the terms of administrative detention provided for by Article 27.5 of the Code of Administrative Offences.
The applicants requested that their lawyers, who had arrived at the Severnoye Izmaylovo District police station and had presented their authority, be allowed to see them.
The applicants' request to see their lawyers at the Severnoye Izmaylovo District police station was refused.
The applicants were not allowed to make a phone call to their families at the Severnoye Izmaylovo District police station.
At the Vostochnyy District police station the applicants requested to see a lawyer and to make a phone call, but this was refused.
The first applicant lodged a complaint about the refusal to see a lawyer and make a phone call at the Vostochnyy District police station.
At 2.30 a.m. on 6 December 2011 the applicants were transferred to the Kitay-Gorod District police station.
At the Kitay-Gorod District police station the applicants requested permission to see their lawyers and to telephone their families, but their requests were refused.

The Justice of the Peace disallowed the following questions put by the first applicant's defence counsel to police officers I. and F.: "What orders did you personally give to Mr Navalnyy?", "Who gave the order to arrest Mr Navalnyy?" and "Why were two policemen's reports identical?".
The first applicant pleaded not guilty and contested the police officers' testimonies in the administrative proceedings.
The first applicant testified that he had been returning from the authorised meeting, walking together with other people, not marching or chanting any slogans.
The first applicant testified that the police had repeatedly obstructed their way and had then arrested them.
The first applicant insisted that he had not received any orders from the police and had not resisted the arrest.
Witness T. testified that he had seen the first applicant's arrest.
Witness T. testified that it had been noisy and he had not heard the police officers giving the first applicant any orders before arresting him.
Witness T. testified that the police had announced through a loudspeaker "Your actions are unlawful" while surrounding a group of people, and had then begun arresting them.
Witness T. testified that he had not seen the first applicant resisting the arrest.
Witness A. testified that he had been walking down Teatralnyy Proyezd and had seen people in uniform arresting the first applicant on the pavement.
Witness A. testified that during the arrest the police had announced through a loudspeaker "Your actions are unlawful".
Witness A. testified that he had not seen the first applicant resisting the police during the arrest.
The first applicant requested that two video recordings of his arrest, shot by witnesses T. and A., be admitted as evidence in the administrative proceedings.
The first applicant requested that the court obtain and examine the video footage which the police had at their disposal.

The requests to admit the video recordings were dismissed on the grounds that the court had no technical means of playing the recordings and that it would be unacceptable to use the devices provided by the defence.
The requests to admit the video recordings were not joined to the case file on the grounds that they had been submitted at the wrong stage of the proceedings.
According to the first applicant, most of the questions put by the defence to the witnesses were disallowed by the Justice of the Peace in his administrative case.
The Justice of the Peace refused to entertain the first applicant's complaints concerning the lack of access to a lawyer after his arrest.
The Justice of the Peace refused to entertain the first applicant's complaints concerning the refusal of a statutory phone call after the arrest.
The Justice of the Peace refused to entertain the first applicant's complaints concerning the allegedly unlawful detention during the first six hours after the arrest.
The Justice of the Peace refused to entertain the first applicant's complaints concerning the seizure of his possessions during the search.
The Justice of the Peace refused to entertain the first applicant's complaints concerning the inhuman and degrading conditions of transfer and of detention at the Kitay-Gorod District police station.
On 6 December 2011 the Justice of the Peace found the first applicant guilty of having disobeyed the lawful order of the police.
The Justice of the Peace based her findings against the first applicant on the witness statements of police officers I. and F., their written reports and the report on the administrative arrest.

The Justice of the Peace dismissed the testimonies of the first applicant, witness A. and witness T. on the grounds that they had contradicted the police officers' testimonies and reports, and that no reasons for mistrusting the latter had been established.
The first applicant was convicted under Article 19.3 of the Code of Administrative Offences and sentenced to fifteen days' administrative detention.

On 6 December 2011 both applicants lodged appeals against their arrest and conviction for the administrative offence, claiming that these had been in breach of domestic law and in violation of the Convention.
In their appeals, the applicants contested the findings of fact made by the first instance as regards the events following their departure from the authorised meeting.

In their appeals, the applicants complained about the refusal of the Justice of the Peace to grant their requests, to admit the video materials as evidence and to call all the witnesses requested by the defence.
In their appeals, the applicants challenged the grounds on which the court had dismissed the testimonies of the applicants and the defence witnesses.
In their appeals, the applicants complained of unlawful detention during the first six hours after their arrest.
In their appeals, the applicants complained of lack of access to a lawyer.
In their appeals, the applicants complained of the conditions in which they had been transferred between the police stations and remanded in custody at the Kitay-Gorod District police station.
On 7 December 2011 the Tverskoy District Court of Moscow examined the applicants' appeals in separate proceedings.
The Tverskoy District Court of Moscow dismissed the complaints about the refusals to hear witnesses and to admit the evidence requested by the applicants.
The Tverskoy District Court of Moscow rejected the applicants' requests to have witnesses called in the appeal proceedings.
The Tverskoy District Court of Moscow rejected the request to admit the video recordings in evidence because of their "unknown provenance".
The Tverskoy District Court of Moscow refused to keep a verbatim record of the hearing because it considered it unnecessary.
The Tverskoy District Court of Moscow granted the request to join a photograph of the first applicant's arrest to the case file.
On 7 December 2011 the Tverskoy District Court of Moscow dismissed the applicants' appeals and upheld the first-instance judgment in both cases, citing the same reasons.
